claims.name: Tim van Beeck
claims.title: Acoustic wave propagation in nematic liquid crystals: modeling, analysis, and discretization
claims.description: Nematic liquid crystals consist of rod-like molecules whose mean orientation, the director, can be rotated by an external electric field. Because sound travels faster along the director, the acoustic response of the medium can be tuned. After a brief overview of my work on structure-preserving finite element methods for incompressible flows and on hybrid discontinuous Galerkin methods for helioseismology, this talk focuses on the modeling, analysis and numerical analysis of time-harmonic wave equations in nematic liquid crystals. For a constant director, sound waves are modeled by the nematic Helmholtz–Korteweg (NHK) equation, a fourth-order, anisotropic augmentation of the Helmholtz equation. I will show how a Cordes condition on the anisotropy yields a Gårding inequality and, in turn, well-posedness, and how these results lead to convergent $C^1$-conforming and hybrid $C^0$-interior penalty discretizations. Numerical examples illustrate the theory. Finally, I will discuss the extension to variable directors, for which a variational approach based on constrained energy minimization appears promising.

claims.name: Alessio Cesarano
claims.title: Shape optimization of electric machines
claims.description: This talk focuses on shape optimization of electric machines with the aid of shape derivatives. The numerical methods presented include steepest-descent algorithms, the adjoint method, and Hilbertian regularization for smoothing shape derivatives. Particular attention is given to the treatment of time-dependent effects present in electric machines, and in particular to rotating electric machines with time-periodic conditions, where a space-time finite element method is used for the approximate solution of the time-dependent state and adjoint equations. In addition, multi-descent shape optimization algorithms and a shape-Newton method are presented for multi-objective shape optimization problems, with the advantages of being able to detect points in so-called non-convex regions of the Pareto front and to trace the Pareto front with a path-following continuation method using second-order shape derivatives, respectively. Finally, mesh-preserving shape optimization algorithms based on Lipschitz transformations and their application to electric machines are presented. This approach does not use the Hilbertian regularization procedure to extract a deformation field that is a descent direction, but instead computes it as the solution of a minimization problem, with the aim of avoiding costly remeshing procedures, often required due to mesh degradation in the course of the optimization process.

claims.name: Zeyi Xu
claims.title: Accelerated Mirror Descent Methods in Scientific Computing
claims.description: Many computational problems require iterates that respect positivity and conservation of mass. Mirror descent methods enforce such structure through a Bregman divergence, and classical solvers such as the Sinkhorn algorithm for optimal transport can be viewed in this way. In this talk, I present accelerated solvers of this type. I begin with a brief overview of our work and its two main applications, entropic optimal transport and the JKO time steps of Wasserstein gradient flows such as the Poisson–Nernst–Planck system. I then discuss these solvers in more details. I show how acceleration can be added to a classical method while keeping its structure, and why the gain grows as the problem becomes harder. I close with possible connections to the group's Bregman-based finite element methods for variational inequalities, and to solvers for nonlinear PDEs. This is joint work with Long Chen.

claims.name: Mansur Shakipov
claims.title: Surface fluids without the saddle-point structure
claims.description: Fluid flow on closed surfaces models lipid vesicles and surfactant-laden interfaces. Standard finite element methods for the surface Stokes equations inherit the saddle-point structure of the problem and must satisfy a discrete inf-sup condition. We take a different route. The commutator between the viscous operator and the surface divergence is a lower-order term involving the Gauss curvature, which yields a pressure Poisson equation; since a closed surface has no boundary, this equation needs no artificial boundary condition. Replacing the incompressibility constraint by the pressure Poisson equation gives a second-order elliptic system for the velocity-pressure pair, which can therefore be discretized with any pair of polynomial degrees, including equal order. We will show how this informal idea survives scrutiny, how it extends to transient Stokes and Navier-Stokes flow, and what practical consequences it brings. This is joint work with R. H. Nochetto.
